clue.text: Fateful lifeline?

parts.note: surface reading: a rope or link that turned out to decide someone's destiny
setter's reading: belonging to the Fates of Greek myth, who spun, measured and cut the strand of each person's life

explanation.walkthrough: The three Fates spin, measure and snip a strand for every mortal, so the line of life they handle is a length of yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth each human life is a single strand spun by the Fates, so the lifeline in their hands is literally spun fibre.

clue.text: Vamp to make good dilapidated JCB

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
something dilapidated is old and worn
a JCB is a British make of mechanical excavator

explanation.surface: A seductress sets out to restore a broken-down excavator.
explanation.walkthrough: JCB is the British brand name so common it stands for any mechanical excavator.
explanation.definitionFit: A vamp is a seductive woman who exploits men, much as a gold digger courts them for their money.

clue.text: Wreck bears out type of destroyer

indicators.note: to wreck something is to smash it up, so the letters that follow are broken and rebuilt

parts.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval tale about a warship being sunk, as the evidence supposedly confirms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyer' tempts a naval reading, and 'bears out' looks like a verb meaning confirms; both words are only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A saboteur deliberately damages machinery or plans, so he is one kind of person who wrecks things.

clue.text: Nasty skin complaint through sprawling outside

indicators.note: sprawling outside means spreading round the exterior, so one word lies around the other

parts.note: by can mean through, as in 'by means of'
an itch is an irritating skin complaint

explanation.surface: A rash that spreads all over the body is an unpleasant thing to have.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitchy describes spiteful, malicious behaviour or remarks, which is what nasty means applied to people.

clue.text: Prison term for quack, say

parts.note: bird is British slang for time in prison, from rhyming slang bird-lime = time
to term something is to call it by a name

explanation.surface: A slang expression for a phoney doctor, or the jail sentence he deserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing bird' is British slang for serving a prison sentence. 'Quack' looks like a fake doctor, but here it is the noise of a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A quack is the sound a duck makes, which is one example of a noise produced by a bird.

clue.text: Treat as skin and bone old king denied sustenance

parts.note: to tan an animal skin is to treat it to make leather
the talus is the ankle bone

explanation.surface: Someone so starved he is all skin and bone, like a king left without food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin and bone' reads as a phrase meaning emaciated, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth King Tantalus was punished by standing beneath fruit and in water that always receded from his reach.

clue.text: US barman serves awkward customer — a Yank

parts.note: a sod is British slang for a difficult, unpleasant person
taken as written
to yank is to pull sharply, to jerk

explanation.surface: An American bartender deals with a difficult American patron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American person, fitting the US setting, but it is the verb for a sharp tug.
explanation.definitionFit: A soda jerk was a worker serving sodas and ice cream at an American drugstore fountain counter.

clue.text: Test for PM?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an assessment of knowledge
second meaning, split as two words: the afternoon is a former morning, once a.m. and no longer

explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like the Prime Minister facing a test, but it is post meridiem; it follows a.m., so it is ex-a.m.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam is a formal test of knowledge, and split in two the word reads as 'former morning', which the afternoon is.

clue.text: Look up an' doon

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading the same going up as coming down shows the word is identical both ways

parts.note: a Scots word for a peep or glance, used here both as the meaning and as the word to be read both ways

explanation.surface: A Scottish instruction to glance up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots spelling 'an' doon' flags that the answer is a Scots word as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Keek is Scots and northern English for a quick peep or a glance.

clue.text: Horse to take you for a ride?

definitions.text: Horse to take you for a ride?

parts.words: Horse to take you for a ride?
parts.note: surface reading: a mount for a pleasant hack
setter's reading: to swindle you, as a substitute horse entered under a false name does to punters

explanation.walkthrough: To take someone for a ride is to cheat them; a horse secretly swapped into a race under another's identity does just that.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringer is a horse fraudulently substituted for another in a race, to deceive bookmakers and gamblers.

clue.text: Barrister has a day to digest case in brief

parts.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for day
the grammatical vocative case, abbreviated
ate is the past tense of eat, and eating is digesting

explanation.surface: A busy lawyer gets one day to master the file on a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' and 'brief' both pull towards law, but the case is grammatical and 'in brief' means shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: An advocate pleads cases in court, the Scottish and general term for a courtroom lawyer like a barrister.

clue.text: Family group, mean and furtive

parts.note: a clan is a group of related families
to destine is to intend or mean something for a purpose

explanation.surface: A stingy, secretive family keeping to itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' reads as stingy beside 'furtive', but it is the verb for intending.
explanation.definitionFit: Clandestine describes something done secretly and stealthily, which is what furtive behaviour is.

clue.text: Rode southern dales — badly chafed

indicators.note: badly means done poorly or out of order, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for southern
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rider crossing the southern valleys ends up with painful rubbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddle sore describes a rider rubbed raw and aching from long hours on horseback, an apt kind of chafing.

clue.text: Paper-chase?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a newspaper circulating across the whole country
second meaning: the Grand ..., the famous British steeplechase

explanation.walkthrough: A paper chase is a cross-country game with a trail of scraps; split in two, it names a newspaper and a horse race. The Grand National is a famous British steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a newspaper sold countrywide, and the National is the shortened name of Britain's best-known steeplechase.

clue.text: Beauty wearing red rose

indicators.note: something worn is clothed by what surrounds it, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
a belle is a beautiful woman

explanation.surface: A lovely woman dressed in scarlet with a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red rose' reads as a flower, but rose is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise up against authority is to rebel, so the past tense rose in that sense means rebelled.

clue.text: Catching Hague out, Lib Dem tee-heed

indicators.note: catching means holding something within, so one piece is surrounded by another

parts.note: LD is the abbreviation for Liberal Democrat

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or out of place, so the name's letters are reworked

parts.note: the surname taken as written

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat giggles on seeing the Conservative leader Hague tripped up.
explanation.walkthrough: William Hague led the Conservative Party when this was set; the Liberal Democrats are a rival British party.
explanation.definitionFit: To tee-hee is to giggle, so tee-heed is a past-tense verb for making that small sound of amusement.

clue.text: House accommodation?

parts.note: surface reading: somewhere to live, a place to stay
setter's reading: accommodation in its financial sense, money advanced to someone, here to buy a house

explanation.walkthrough: Accommodation looks like lodging, but bankers use it for an advance of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortgage is money lent for buying a property, and lending money is an old financial sense of accommodation.

clue.text: Waste time after game swings back

indicators.note: after places one piece behind the other in the finished word
swinging back means turning round to face the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: brag is a card game similar to poker
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Time is wasted after a game swings back the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Garbage is rubbish thrown away, which is a common noun sense of waste.

clue.text: Enter finally into agreement in spite of underhand dealings

indicators.note: into means going inside, so one piece is placed within another
in places what precedes it inside the following word

parts.note: malice is spite, the wish to do harm
a pact is a formal agreement

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of that word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone signs a contract despite knowing about crooked practices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In spite of' reads as one phrase meaning despite, but it splits into 'in', 'spite' and the link 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Malpractice is improper or illegal professional conduct, the kind of dishonest behaviour underhand dealings describes.

clue.text: Leg's game — in car crash with learner

indicators.note: in places the preceding piece inside the following one
a crash leaves the vehicle mangled, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
RU is rugby union
L is for learner, from the plates on British learner drivers' cars

explanation.surface: A learner driver crashes the car and hurts a leg in the process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg's' works as an adjective here: crural means of the leg, as in 'the leg's muscles'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crural is the anatomical adjective for the leg or thigh, so it means belonging to the leg.

clue.text: Reeled from second stomach upset

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a maw is an animal's stomach or gullet

explanation.surface: Someone staggers after a second bout of stomach upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach upset' looks like indigestion; here 'upset' turns the word over.
explanation.definitionFit: When your head swam you felt dizzy and giddy, which is what reeled means in that sense.

clue.text: Likes making nasty remarks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for enjoys or appreciates

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys being spiteful.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang to dig something is to enjoy it, and a dig is also a pointed, cutting jibe at someone.

clue.text: Cat with another injury

parts.note: the cat o' nine tails is a whip
another word for the same cat: a lash

explanation.surface: One cat fights another and ends up hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' is the cat o' nine tails, the flogging whip, and 'another' asks for a second word for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiplash is a neck injury caused by the head being jerked violently, as in a car collision.

clue.text: One may smoke over a packet

definitions.text: One may smoke over a packet

parts.words: One may smoke over a packet
parts.note: surface reading: a smoker lighting up from a pack of cigarettes
setter's reading: a packet boat, a steamer carrying mail and passengers, with smoke rising above it

explanation.walkthrough: A packet was a scheduled mail steamer; the chimney on deck is what smokes above it.
explanation.definitionFit: On a steamship the tall chimney venting smoke from the boilers is called by this name, standing above the deck.

clue.text: Mutilated carcases, with initial number up 900, reveal the slaughter

indicators.note: something mutilated is cut up and disfigured, so its letters are scrambled
the opening Roman numeral is raised by nine hundred, swapping one numeral letter for a larger one

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Butchered bodies and a sharply rising death toll expose a bloodbath.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter C is 100 in Roman numerals; adding 900 makes 1,000, which is M.
explanation.definitionFit: A massacre is the brutal killing of many people at once, which is what slaughter means as a noun.

clue.text: Back in bed, sick and wan

indicators.note: in places the following word inside the bed word

parts.note: a pad is slang for a bed or place to sleep

indicators.note: back means going the opposite way, so the combined letters read right to left

parts.note: ill means sick

explanation.surface: Someone back in bed with illness, looking pale.
explanation.definitionFit: Pallid and wan both describe a pale, sickly complexion lacking healthy colour.
